cues.text: Let us close this study session with exam consolidation.
The goal is to pull together what you have learned about documents, records, ownership and communication, and to check that you can use it under exam conditions.
The first skill is to distinguish document types and their uses across the lifecycle.
In an exam, never just name a document.
Say what it is for, who reads it, and at which phase it matters.
A requirements document records what stakeholders need, so it matters most early on.
A design document records how the system will be structured, so it guides implementation.
A test document records what will be checked and what was found, so it supports verification and release decisions.
Operational and maintenance records support the system once it is live.
A strong answer links each document to a lifecycle phase and to a decision it supports.
Next come quality attributes.
These describe how well a system does its job, not only what it does.
Be ready to name an attribute, define it in one clear sentence, and say how you would recognise whether it has been met.
Examiners often ask you to separate attributes that sound alike, so always anchor your definition to an observable behaviour.
Now version control.
Its purpose is to keep a reliable history of changes: what changed, who changed it, when, and why.
It lets a team return to an earlier state, compare versions, and work in parallel without silently overwriting each other.
Version control applies to code, and also to the documents that describe the work.
If a requirement or design document exists in several unlabelled copies, nobody can say which one is current.
That leads to traceability, which means being able to follow a link in both directions.
You can go from a stakeholder need to its requirement, then to the design element, the code, and the test that checks it.
You can also go back the other way, from a failing test to the requirement it protects.
Traceability shows that nothing was forgotten, and it shows the impact of a change, because you can see what else is connected to it.
Then there is RACI, a way of assigning ownership.
R stands for Responsible, the person who does the work.
A stands for Accountable, the person who answers for the outcome and approves it.
C stands for Consulted, someone whose input is sought before a decision.
I stands for Informed, someone who is told the result.
Be careful with the distinction between Responsible and Accountable, because it is commonly confused.
Many people may do the work, but accountability should rest with one clear owner.
When ownership is unclear, tasks are assumed to belong to someone else and never get done.
Communication comes next.
Synchronous communication happens in real time, with everyone present together, such as a live meeting or call.
It suits urgent issues, fast clarification and sensitive discussions.
Asynchronous communication does not require simultaneous presence.
Messages, comments and documents are read and answered later.
It suits distributed teams in different time zones, gives people time to think, and leaves a written record.
Neither is always better.
Choose according to urgency, complexity and the need for a record.
Collaboration tools support both styles.
They hold shared documents, task tracking, discussion and code review in one place, so the team works from the same information.
Connecting such tools to one another, or to other systems, brings the need for secure integrations.
Every connection is a possible route for exposure.
So integrations should be given only the access they need, their credentials should be protected and kept out of shared records, and who approved the connection should be known.
A convenient integration that is not controlled can become a weakness.
Now bring these threads together, because the exam asks you to explain how good records and ownership prevent ambiguity, recurring defects and unsafe releases.
Ambiguity is prevented because a clear, current, versioned record means everyone reads the same statement of what is needed, so they do not each interpret it differently.
Recurring defects are prevented because a recorded defect, with its cause and its fix, can be traced and learned from.
Without a record, the team may fix the symptom, forget it, and meet the same problem again.
Unsafe releases are prevented because a named owner is accountable for approving a release, and because records show that the required tests and reviews were actually completed.
Without ownership and records, a release can go out simply because everyone assumed someone else had checked.
The final skill is to apply calculations and interpret metrics, with their limitations.
When you calculate, write out the formula, substitute the values exactly as given, keep the units, and show each step.
Then comes interpretation, which is where many students lose marks.
A number alone is not a conclusion.
Ask what the metric actually measures, what it does not measure, and what could make it misleading, such as a small sample, a short period, or definitions that differ between teams.
A good answer states the result, explains what it suggests, and states plainly what the metric cannot prove.
Do not claim more than the figures support.
